analysis.body:
Finance and insurance firms report AI use at 36.8%, up from 35.5% in the prior period, making it one of the more measurable adoption stories available, though the figure covers the broader finance and insurance category rather than depository banking alone. The headline number is also somewhat misleading as a gauge of novelty: fraud detection and credit underwriting models have run under regulatory oversight for decades, meaning a portion of what the survey captures is mature, well-understood technology rather than recent deployments of generative or large-language-model tools. The genuinely new frontier, as the sector's own framing makes clear, is generative AI applied to customer service and compliance workflows.

The governance infrastructure here is older and more developed than in almost any other sector. The Federal Reserve's SR 11-7 guidance, issued in 2011, established model risk management requirements that now apply directly to AI systems used in credit decisions and anti-money-laundering processes, meaning banking entered the current AI boom with a supervisory framework already in place rather than scrambling to build one. Treasury has since mapped the broader risk surface for AI in financial services, framing the US supervisory conversation around uses, opportunities, and specific risks, and that framing shapes what examiners look for and what compliance teams must document.

On the competitive intelligence side, the Evident AI Banking Index provides the closest thing the industry has to a public scoreboard, scoring major global banks across maturity metrics that span talent, innovation, leadership, and transparency. That kind of structured benchmarking matters because it makes relative positioning legible to investors, regulators, and peers in a way that self-reported surveys cannot. Financial-domain-specific models are also tracked and catalogued separately from general-purpose systems, reflecting the practical reality that models tuned on financial text behave differently enough from general models to warrant distinct provenance and evaluation records.

For anyone deciding whether to deploy AI in a banking context, the record suggests the question is less whether to adopt and more whether the governance scaffolding is in place before deployment. SR 11-7 compliance is not optional, and examiners have long experience stress-testing model validation practices. The concentration of documented risk and regulatory attention around credit models and AML means those are the highest-scrutiny deployment zones, while customer-facing generative applications occupy a somewhat less settled supervisory space, one that Treasury's ongoing work is actively trying to define.
